summary: Packed onto just 7.6 square miles immediately south of San Francisco, Daly City crams over 100,000 people at a density north of 13,000 per square mile — making it one of the most densely populated cities in California that almost nobody outside the Bay Area thinks about. The terrain rises sharply from the coastal bluffs above the Pacific, where fog rolls through neighborhoods stacked on hillsides so steeply that houses appear to sit on each other's roofs — a landscape Malvina Reynolds reportedly had in mind when she wrote "Little Boxes." That fog-cooled microclimate holds average daytime highs to a remarkably steady 62°F year-round, meaning you'll rarely sweat and rarely shiver, but you may go weeks in summer without seeing the sun until afternoon. Functionally, this is a bedroom community: BART's Daly City station anchors the western terminus of the system, funneling commuters into San Francisco's Financial District in under 20 minutes, and the city itself has no single dominant employer sector to absorb the workforce locally. At a median household income of roughly $120K, the median home price of nearly $1.1 million puts the price-to-income ratio above 9:1 — firmly in stretch territory for buyers, while median rent of $2,523 consumes about a quarter of that gross income, comparatively moderate by Peninsula standards. The food and grocery landscape punches well above what most pass-through visitors expect, with a dense concentration of sit-down restaurants, bakeries, and specialty grocery stores lining Mission Street and Junipero Serra Boulevard. Daly City is the place where a San Francisco commute meets fog-belt affordability — relatively speaking — but the tradeoff is a city whose identity has always been defined more by what it's next to than by what it contains.
